claims.text: Elevated-temperature structural stability in nearly equiatomic five-component transition-metal HENA is governed by competition between configurational entropy and surface-energy minimization.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase solid solution in these nanoparticles.
Surface-energy minimization drives phase segregation in these nanoparticles.
Below a critical particle diameter, the surface-energy contribution dominates because of the increased surface-to-volume ratio.
Surface-energy dominance below the critical diameter causes conversion from a single-phase solid solution to a core-shell or multiphase structure.
The proposed size-dependent structural transition is not predicted by bulk thermodynamic models.
The component with the lowest surface energy preferentially diffuses and segregates to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation reduces total surface free energy.
Surface segregation lowers the activation barrier for nucleation of secondary phases in the nanoparticle core.
Preferential surface segregation changes the composition of the nanoparticle core.
The segregation-induced change in core composition can move the core outside the single-phase region of the phase diagram.
A core composition outside the single-phase region can undergo spinodal decomposition or nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
Nanoparticles below the critical diameter will develop core-shell structures or distinct phase separation after annealing.
Bulk samples of the same composition will remain single-phase under conditions where subcritical nanoparticles segregate.
Segregation in the nanoparticles will begin at lower temperatures than in the corresponding bulk alloy.
Segregation in the nanoparticles will occur on shorter timescales than in the corresponding bulk alloy.
The segregating species will have an anomalously high surface diffusion coefficient.

Traditional alloying concepts and bulk CALPHAD models predict that equiatomic alloys with five or more components remain stable single-phase solid solutions up to melting when mixing-enthalpy penalties are insignificant.
Particles larger than the critical diameter are expected to be governed primarily by bulk configurational entropy rather than surface energy.
Systems whose components have nearly identical surface energies should not exhibit significant preferential surface segregation.
